briefOverview: Simeon urges his descendants to renounce envy and pride, presenting a sweeping vision of peace and divine salvation centered in Levi and Judah. The chapter closes with Simeon’s death and a brief narrative about the handling of the patriarchs’ bones in Egypt before the Exodus.
summary:
Simeon frames his instruction as a final attempt to be “acquitted” of his children’s sin, calling them to remove envy and “stiff-neckedness.” He promises that if they do so, his line will flourish in Israel with imagery of flowers, fragrance, and cedars, and “holy ones” multiplying from him.

The chapter then shifts into an eschatological vision: hostile peoples and lands are said to perish, the earth rests from trouble and war, and God appears on earth to save humanity, subduing deceitful spirits. Simeon rejoices that God “hath taken a body and eaten with men,” and he instructs his children to obey Levi and Judah, because salvation will arise through them—depicted as a High Priest from Levi and a King from Judah who is “God and man” and who saves Gentiles and Israel alike.

Finally, Simeon dies at 120 years old; his body is placed in a wooden coffin to be taken to Hebron. The text recounts that his bones were moved secretly during an Egyptian war, alongside a tradition that Egyptians guarded Joseph’s bones due to ominous predictions, and it concludes by noting that Simeon’s descendants remained in Egypt until the departure under Moses.
externalContext: The Testament of Simeon is part of the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, a collection often dated to the Second Temple period and preserved chiefly through later manuscripts; many scholars consider the work to have undergone Christian editing or interpolation, especially where it explicitly describes God appearing on earth and “taking a body.” The setting is presented as Simeon’s deathbed discourse to his sons, echoing the genre of patriarchal “testaments” found in Jewish and early Christian literature. The emphasis on Levi (priesthood) and Judah (kingship) reflects long-standing Israelite institutions associated with the Jerusalem temple and the Davidic monarchy, later developed in messianic expectation. The notice about bones being taken to Hebron draws on ancestral burial traditions tied to the patriarchs and the region around Hebron (Machpelah).
externalReferences:
The promise of a ruler from Judah resonates with Jacob’s blessing in Genesis 49:10, while the expectation of a priestly figure aligns with the prominence of Levi in priestly texts (e.g., Deuteronomy 33:8–11). The claim that the Lord “shall appear on earth” and “taken a body and eaten with men” reads like an incarnation motif, closely paralleling New Testament christological themes such as John 1:14.

The closing notice that Simeon’s descendants remained in Egypt until the departure “by the hand of Moses” corresponds to the Exodus tradition (Exodus 12:40–41). The concern for transporting patriarchal bones evokes Genesis 50:25 and Joshua 24:32 regarding Joseph’s remains.
practicalQuestions: What forms of envy most commonly distort my relationships, and what concrete practices would help me “remove” it?
How do pride and “stiff-neckedness” show up in my refusal to listen or be corrected, and what would repentance look like in a specific situation?
What does it mean, in my context, to honor legitimate spiritual and communal leadership without becoming “lifted up against” others?
If the text’s vision is that God acts to end war and deceit, how might I contribute to peace and truthfulness in my immediate circles (work, family, community)?
uncertainAreas: The identity and function of the listed nations/lands (Canaan, Amalek, Cappadocians, Hittites, Ham) in vv. 3–4 is unclear: the text reads as a generalized judgment-oracle, but the precise historical referent may be symbolic or anachronistic. The explicitly incarnational language in v. 9 and the “God and man” phrasing in v. 11 may reflect later Christian interpolation, but determining that from this chapter alone is uncertain. The narrative about Egyptian sorcerers and Joseph’s bones (vv. 14–15) appears to be an expanded tradition beyond the biblical account; its provenance cannot be verified from the passage itself.
